items.followUp: Why does atomic radius generally decrease from left to right across a period?

rubric.why: Identifies the subshell receiving the differentiating electron.
rubric.description: The last (differentiating) electron enters a p subshell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the differentiating electron enters a p subshell or p orbital.

rubric.why: Connects the p-block classification to the relevant groups.
rubric.description: This applies to elements in groups 13 to 18.

modelAnswer: Elements of groups 13 to 18 are called p-block elements because their differentiating (last) electron enters a p subshell.
Helium is an exception because its last electron enters an s subshell.

items.followUp: Why does atomic size generally decrease across a period?

rubric.why: States the cause of the stronger attraction across a period.
rubric.description: Nuclear charge increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting the increase in nuclear or effective nuclear charge.

rubric.why: States how the increased nuclear charge affects an added electron.
rubric.description: The nucleus attracts an added electron more strongly, so electron affinity generally increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking stronger attraction to increased electron affinity.

modelAnswer: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while the added electron enters the same main energy level.
The nucleus attracts the added electron more strongly, so electron affinity generally increases from left to right.

items.followUp: What is a double covalent bond? Give an example.

rubric.why: Identifies how many electron pairs are shared.
rubric.description: A triple covalent bond involves the sharing of three pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that three electron pairs are shared.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a triple covalent bond.
rubric.description: Nitrogen molecule (N₂) contains a triple covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving nitrogen (N₂) as an example.

modelAnswer: A triple covalent bond is formed when two atoms share three pairs of electrons.
For example, the two nitrogen atoms in N₂ are joined by a triple bond (N≡N).

items.followUp: State how an atom can complete its octet by forming an ionic bond.

rubric.why: States the stable outer-shell arrangement described by the rule.
rubric.description: Atoms tend to attain eight electrons in their valence shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the valence shell becomes complete with eight electrons.

rubric.why: Names the ways atoms achieve the stable arrangement.
rubric.description: Atoms gain, lose, or share electrons to attain the octet.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning gain, loss, or sharing of electrons.

modelAnswer: The octet rule states that atoms gain, lose, or share electrons to attain eight electrons in their valence shell.
This gives them a stable outer-shell arrangement.

items.followUp: What are crystalline solids? Give an example.

rubric.why: Identifies the characteristic arrangement of particles in an amorphous solid.
rubric.description: The constituent particles are not arranged in a regular pattern.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the particles as irregularly or randomly arranged.

rubric.description: Glass is a common example of an amorphous solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a valid example such as glass.

modelAnswer: Amorphous solids are solids whose constituent particles are not arranged in a regular pattern.
Glass is an example of an amorphous solid.

items.followUp: Define a solute and give an example.

rubric.why: Identifies the uniform nature of a solution.
rubric.description: A solution is a homogeneous (uniform) mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a solution as a homogeneous or uniform mixture.

rubric.why: Identifies the components of a solution.
rubric.description: A solution consists of a solute dissolved in a solvent; for example, salt dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning solute and solvent, or giving a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute and a solvent.
For example, salt dissolved in water forms a salt solution.

items.followUp: What types of substances dissolve best in polar solvents?

rubric.why: Expresses the similarity principle behind the rule.
rubric.description: Substances with similar properties, especially similar polarity, tend to dissolve in one another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substances have similar properties or polarity.

rubric.why: Gives the practical meaning of the rule.
rubric.description: Polar substances dissolve in polar solvents, while non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving either valid polar/non-polar pairing.

modelAnswer: “Like dissolves like” means that substances with similar properties, especially similar polarity, dissolve in one another.
Thus, polar substances dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.

items.followUp: Name two metals commonly used in jewellery.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming platinum or another valid noble metal.

modelAnswer: Two noble metals are gold and platinum.
